slides.title: Multi-cloud Systems
slides.raw:
Multi-cloud Systems
• Reduced single points of failure
• Enhanced security
• Flexibility and scalability
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Computing resources delivered on demand from a provider rather than entirely owned and operated locally.

course.learn: A multi-cloud strategy uses services from more than one cloud provider. It can reduce dependency on one provider and support specialized capabilities, but it increases operational and security complexity.
course.why: Different IAM, logging, networking, and security tooling can make consistent controls harder.
course.example: A company runs customer-facing applications in one cloud and analytics workloads in another while centralizing identity and logging.
course.exam: Multi-cloud is not automatically redundant unless workloads/data can actually fail over across providers.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Continuity of Operations (COOP) planning defines how essential functions continue during disruption, including people, alternate facilities, communications, technology, and procedures.
course.why: Business continuity is broader than restoring one server; it keeps the organization's critical mission functioning.
course.example: If headquarters is unavailable, designated staff move to an alternate site and use documented procedures to continue priority services.
course.exam: COOP/business continuity focuses on essential operations; disaster recovery is more technology-recovery focused.
